title: The wretched man (Romans 7:14–25)
hook: the good I want, I don't do

segments.voice: Yesterday, dead to sin, baptism as a burial and a rising, and your line was newness of life. Did you try your one new habit? If it wobbled already, today is for you. Day three hundred nineteen.

It's eleven at night. You promised yourself you'd be in bed by ten. You know exactly why you should put the phone down. You want to put the phone down. And your thumb keeps scrolling, as if it belongs to someone else. Or it's the sharp word you swore you wouldn't say, and there it is, out of your mouth again. Everybody knows this feeling: wanting one thing and doing another. What's surprising is to find it in the middle of a letter by one of the most driven people in history. Right after Paul's big picture of new life, he writes one of the most honest paragraphs in the whole letter.
screen: `ELEVEN AT NIGHT, STILL SCROLLING.` → `WANTING ONE THING, DOING ANOTHER.` → `PAUL'S MOST HONEST PARAGRAPH.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." Read it twice and you'll hear yourself. Paul says he agrees with God's law. He delights in it. He knows it's good. And still, something in him pulls the other way, like a second law at war inside him. The knowing isn't the problem. The doing is. Then the paragraph breaks open into a cry: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Wretched, in Greek talaiporos, means worn down, miserable, like someone exhausted by a long hardship. It isn't a pose. It's a groan. And notice the question he asks. Not how do I fix myself, but who shall deliver me? He's looking outside himself. And the answer comes in the very next breath: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." Now here's a real puzzle, and Christians have argued over it for many centuries: who is this I? Some readers, including Augustine in his later years and Martin Luther, hear Paul describing the Christian life: even the baptized still feel this war inside, every day. Many early Greek teachers, and many scholars today, hear Paul speaking about life under the law without the Spirit, the way things look before chapter eight. The text doesn't settle it for us. But almost every reader recognizes the feeling. Paul's letter doesn't hide the struggle or scold it. It names it, and it cries out for help.
screen: `THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.` · `TWO LAWS AT WAR INSIDE.` · `WHO SHALL DELIVER ME?` · `WHO IS THIS I?` · then, large: `O WRETCHED MAN THAT I AM!`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be gentle with your own struggle. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing you keep doing that you don't want to do. Something small and real. Instead of the usual lecture you give yourself, try speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend who told you the same thing. Tired. Honest. Still trying. Notice where the struggle sits in your body, and let your breath go there. If you pray, you can say Paul's own question, who shall deliver me, and just wait with it. The bell holds the time.
The wretched man. Paul's cry, talaiporos in Greek: worn down by the war between the good he wants and what he does.

Your line: who shall deliver me? Today, when you catch yourself doing the thing you didn't want to do, skip the lecture. Take one breath, and ask for help, from God or from a friend. Day three hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 7 when talking honestly about habits and temptation, in confession, in recovery groups and in spiritual direction, where the struggle is named without shame.

original.note: Greek: wretched, worn down, miserable from long hardship.

trapdoor: what you thought: the wretched man is someone who hates himself.
what it means: Paul names the war between the good he wants and what he does, and cries out for someone to deliver him.
what a scholar hears: whether this I is Paul the Christian, Paul before Christ, or a voice for Adam or Israel is among the most debated questions in reading Romans.

notes: Interpretive history: Augustine's later reading (e.g. against the Pelagians) and Luther's (simul iustus et peccator) take the 'I' as the Christian; many Greek Fathers and many modern scholars (following e.g. Kümmel, 1929) take it as life under the law. Confirm the summary 'many early Greek teachers'.
Changed 'sixteen centuries' to 'many centuries': the debate predates Augustine (Origen already discusses the speaker of Romans 7 in the 3rd century).
Softened 'the most honest paragraph in the whole letter' to 'one of the most honest paragraphs' (evaluative superlative).
Talaiporos glossed as worn down by hardship; confirm.
Practice invites saying Paul's own words ('who shall deliver me') if one prays; this is a scripture line, not a new prayer.
